ai.definition: Smart automation refers to the integration of advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, and IoT into operational systems to enable autonomous optimization and decision-making.
ai.howItWorks: Through a closed-loop system, sensors collect real-time data which is analyzed by AI algorithms. Based on this analysis, automated systems adjust their operations in real time to optimize performance or achieve specific goals without human intervention.
ai.problemSolved: Manual adjustments and inefficiencies common in traditional operational systems are reduced or eliminated, leading to improved efficiency, cost savings, and enhanced productivity.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing processes become more flexible and responsive through the use of smart automation. This includes predictive maintenance, quality control, and dynamic resource allocation.
ai.buildProcess: The development involves designing AI models, integrating IoT devices, and deploying software that can interpret data and make real-time decisions. Testing is crucial to ensure reliability and safety.
ai.costDrivers: Initial high costs due to advanced technology adoption, ongoing maintenance and data processing expenses, and potential cybersecurity risks.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for smart automation is positive as more industries recognize its benefits. However, challenges such as data privacy and security need to be addressed before widespread adoption.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by region but generally focus on data protection, cybersecurity, and ensuring the safety of automated systems in critical applications like healthcare or transportation.
ai.risks: Cybersecurity threats, data privacy concerns, integration challenges with existing infrastructure, and potential job displacement are significant risks.
ai.profitability: Potential for high profitability as companies can reduce costs and increase efficiency. However, initial investment may deter some businesses from adopting early on.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments could include more sophisticated AI capabilities, greater integration across different industries, and enhanced focus on ethical considerations in automation.

glossary.def: A system where the output is continuously monitored and used to adjust the input for optimal performance.
The development of computer systems that can perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence, such as learning, problem-solving, and decision-making.
A network of physical devices, vehicles, appliances, and other items embedded with sensors, software, and connectivity to exchange data and perform actions.

subsystems.name: Sensing and instrumentation
subsystems.role: measures what the process is actually doing — flow, temperature, pressure, position, vibration, energy draw.

subsystems.name: Controllers
subsystems.role: runs the fast closed loop that keeps the machine or process inside safe operating limits.

subsystems.name: Industrial network
subsystems.role: carries measurements up and setpoints down with predictable timing.

subsystems.name: Supervisory and data layer
subsystems.role: gives operators a live picture and stores history for analysis.

subsystems.name: Optimisation and models
subsystems.role: decides the better setpoints — the layer that makes it 'smart' rather than merely automated.
parts: machine-learning models for prediction and anomaly detection

buildSteps.title: Map the process
buildSteps.detail: Document every measurement, actuator and constraint, and decide which variables are safe to move automatically.

buildSteps.title: Instrument it
buildSteps.detail: Fit sensors and, where needed, upgrade actuators and drives so the system can actually be steered.

buildSteps.title: Connect it
buildSteps.detail: Build the control network and the data path upward, so the same measurements serve both the fast loop and the analytics.

buildSteps.title: Automate the loop
buildSteps.detail: Write control logic — classic PID loops first, then sequences — and tune it against real disturbances.

buildSteps.title: Build the model
buildSteps.detail: Create a digital twin or fitted data model of the process, calibrated on logged history.

buildSteps.title: Add the optimiser
buildSteps.detail: Layer model-predictive or learning-based control on top, generating setpoints for the loops beneath.

buildSteps.title: Run in shadow mode
buildSteps.detail: Let the optimiser propose actions while humans still decide, and compare its choices with what operators do.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop with limits
buildSteps.detail: Hand over increasing authority, with hard safety envelopes, fallback to base control, and continuous monitoring for drift.

prerequisites.tech: Cheap, reliable industrial sensors and IIoT
prerequisites.why: optimisation is only as good as the data feeding it.
control decisions must arrive on time; jitter causes instability.
models and optimisers need processing close to the plant and capacity for training.

prerequisites.tech: Validated process models and control theory
prerequisites.why: model-predictive control works well on well-understood processes, less so on poorly characterised ones.
connecting operational technology to networks creates attack paths that must be defended.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop automation and model-predictive control in refineries, power plants, mines and factories
pathway.unlocks: steadier output, lower energy use per unit, fewer manual interventions.

pathway.milestone: learning-based optimisation layered on top of existing control, supervised by operators
pathway.unlocks: gains in processes too complex to model from first principles.

pathway.milestone: self-optimising plant sections that retune themselves as equipment wears and feedstocks change
pathway.unlocks: fewer engineers needed per unit of output, and faster response to disturbances.

pathway.milestone: supervised autonomous operation across whole sites, with human oversight
pathway.unlocks: round-the-clock operation in remote or hazardous locations — bounded by safety cases and regulation.
